doc.title: George Russell — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Taking Bill Evans to Miles Davis's band in Brooklyn
summary: He drove Bill Evans and Barry Galbraith to a Bed-Stuy club where Miles gave Bill Red Garland's chair at intermission, leading to Kind of Blue.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: You – if I’m not mistaken, when Miles was looking for a piano player, you recommended Bill to him, didn’t you?
Yes I did. I took Barry Galbraith, a great guitar player, and Bill, put them in the car, a – those German cars. What were they called? Little small cars. We went over . . .
Volkswagens?
Yeah – went over to a club in Brooklyn, hot club. Miles had told me that he was looking for a piano player, he said, “because these guys – my band are messing me up,” missing airplanes and stuff.
He was having a lot of problems with that at that point, and he had cleaned up his act.

And he was looking for a new way to play. Bill already had that new way, the modal approach. The band was a great band, but with Philly Joe in – I never – I sat in with him once. It’s like, wow, the energy was just amazing, but Philly Joe was missing planes. There’s a fat kid that played . . .
Played what? What instrument are you talking about?
Played tenor.
Tenor?
Yeah.
I thought you meant Cannonball, but . . .
Cannonball. That’s who I’m talking about.
Oh okay, alto, yeah.
The piano player was . . .
Red [Garland].
. . . Red, who I loved. I loved Red. He didn’t – I guess he was pulling too many missed planes.
Yeah, I was going to say, he had this thing as well.
Bass player was excellent.
A youngster.
So, at intermission, Miles gave Bill Red’s chair.
Wow, right at intermission.
Yeah.
That’s the way it goes down lots of times.
It was beautiful. At the end Miles told Bill – he said, “You’re going with us on Saturday to Philadelphia.” That’s the way it happened. I forget the name of the club out there.

Yeah, I was trying to think of what clubs were out in Brooklyn during that time. The only one I can think of, I’m sure isn’t the one, is there used to be a club out there called the Blue Coronet that I always liked. But you’ll think of it. When you do, we’ll fill it in somewhere, not necessarily on the tape.
Bed-Stuy.
Bed-Stuy?
Yeah, that’s where it was.
Wow, that was historic. Bill was happy, wasn’t he?
You couldn’t tell about Bill. That was one thing.
Was he deadpan? Or stoic? Or just so low-key that . . . ? How would you characterize it?
I think he was maybe a bit uncomfortable, because he was out of his element. He wasn’t used to . . .
The club scene and a lot of black guys, Miles.
He wasn’t used to the likes of Red and . . .
. . . Philly.
Yeah, Cannonball.
He sure played beautifully in that group though. Man, that was one of the great groups of all time.
It had to be, because the records they made with Bill are still the best-selling records.
